top_strength: The estimate work was genuinely good and is the reason this call scores where it does. She asked the two questions that actually predict the clock on this job — distance from the current unit to the elevator, and distance from the elevator to the new unit — caught the 100-yard walk, and then used it explicitly in the quote: 'I would estimate it to take about maybe three to five hours since there's gonna be a long walk at the new place.' She also probed oversized/heavy items, valuables and artwork, and appliances, and when the customer could not guess a box count she anchored him with a real benchmark ('typically a three bedroom apartment usually has 35 to 45 pre-pack boxes'). Her honesty on the 2.5-hour minimum — telling him the crew may genuinely have to leave if someone is booked after him — is what moved him from 2.5 hours to booking four.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix is the Save Your Ass speech, and on this call it was free money. The customer volunteered 'we'll certainly box up as much as we can' and is moving inside the same complex — the exact language should have been: 'Since you're staying in the same building, anything you can walk over or take in a carload before move day comes straight off your bill. Consolidate the loose stuff — kids' toys, garden tools, anything in drawers, photos off the walls — into boxes ahead of time, and every trip the guys don't make is fifteen minutes you don't pay for. Does that make sense?' That is a direct hit on estimate accuracy and it costs thirty seconds. Second priority: she quoted a two-hour arrival window and never paired it with the On-Time Guarantee — any time a window leaves her mouth, 'and if we miss that window we start discounting immediately' has to follow it. Third, clean up the readback. He repeated the afternoon window back as '12:30 to 3:30' twice and she let it stand; before ending a booking call, restate date, start window, hours reserved, and address once and have the customer confirm. Credit where it is due — Meet Your Mover, no deposit, the confirmation email, and the long-walk-driven estimate were all there, which is more than most calls this month.
phone_presence_notes: Strong on name use (five-plus natural uses of 'Jeremy') and the customer closed warm with 'thank you so much,' but the language was mechanical and affirmation-light — no empathy statements, no rapport or humor, and several exchanges where the customer had to say 'say that again' or misheard times without being smoothly corrected.
audio_review_reason: The customer asked her to repeat herself multiple times and misread the arrival window back twice, and the transcript is heavily garbled on key numbers ('a $2 for minimum', 'reti base', '12:30 AM'); audio is needed to tell whether this is pace and enunciation or just ASR noise.
